The Shuowen Jiezi explains: "The character bo means a horse of impure color." Among the Tuyuhun horses, those with such an uneven, bluish-mottled coat were called Qingbo, or Azure Piebalds.
Legends say the Ganlong region produced fine "Qin Horses" as early as the Qin Dynasty. Later, the Tuyuhun people settled there to graze their herds. According to the Book of Sui, a myth tells of a Persian stallion that bred with a local mare near Qinghai Lake, producing a Cong colt that could run a thousand li a day. This legendary colt became known as the Tuyuhun Horse.
Muscular and well-proportioned, the Tuyuhun Horse is strong yet gentle and easy to train. These horses are highly social, moving in herds led by a dominant stallion. With keen ears and sharp eyes, they are intelligent, alert, and fiercely loyal to both their kind and their master. Suited for riding and light draft work, they became one of the most common breeds in the Central Plains.

In the age of chaos after the Liang Dynasty fell, warlords vied for supremacy. So great was the slaughter that rivers were choked with bones, and plague-bearing vermin festered across the land.

A fellowship of heroes begged an immortal for aid. To show their unwavering resolve, the immortal laughed, destroyed their own mountain grotto, and strode forth to join the cause.

Years later, the land was cleansed, save for a single great toad demon lurking in the Poison Abyss. The immortal descended into the depths, bearing the Ever-burning Lamp to suppress the beast. At the climax of their battle, the lamp was extinguished. In its place, a brilliant silhouette appeared as the very mountain shattered and a pure spring erupted forth. The demon was sealed forever in the abyss, which, purified by the sacrifice, was henceforth known as the Gleaming Abyss.

Having perfected their path, the immortal ascended to the heavens. And in eternal gratitude, the heroes chronicled the epic in the Tales of Immortals. To this day, the common folk honor the sacrifice by lighting lamps and praying to the Big Dipper on the new and full moons.

An ode commemorates the immortal's lesson: Only through worship can one glimpse immortality.
